ety.text: From Middle English of, from Old English of (“from, out of, off”), an unstressed form of æf, from Proto-West Germanic *ab, from Proto-Germanic *ab (“away; away from”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epó (“away”). Doublet of off, which is the stressed descendant of the same Old English word. More at off.

ex: Take the chicken out of the freezer.
Against headache, vertigo, vapours which ascend forth of the stomach to molest the head, read Hercules de Saxonia and others.

senses.d: Since, from (a given time, earlier state etc.).
ex: He hasn't been well of late.
And he axed his father: howe longe is it agoo, sens this hath happened hym? And he sayde, of a chylde.

senses.d: From, away from (a position, number, distance etc.).
ex: There are no shops within twenty miles of the cottage.

senses.d: Indicating removal, absence or separation, with the action indicated by a transitive verb and the quality or substance by a grammatical object.
ex: Finally she was relieved of the burden of caring for her sick husband.

senses.d: Indicating removal, absence or separation, with resulting state indicated by an adjective.
ex: He seemed devoid of human feelings.
But schemes are perfectly accidental: some will appear barren of hints and matter, but prove to be fruitful […]

senses.d: Indicating removal, absence or separation, construed with an intransitive verb.
ex: He was kindly treated by the people at Saco, and recovered of his wounds.

senses.d: Indicating an ancestral source or origin of descent.
ex: The word is believed to be of Japanese origin.
My father was born of a family of weavers in Manchester, England.

senses.d: Introducing an epithet that indicates a birthplace, residence, dominion, or other place associated with the individual.
Indicating a (non-physical) source of action or emotion; introducing a cause, instigation; from, out of, as an expression of.
ex: The invention was born of necessity.
Undoubtedly it is to be understood, that inflicting deserved punishment on all evil doers, of right, belongs to God.

senses.d: Indicates the source or cause of the verb.
ex: It is said that she died of a broken heart.
He smelled of beer and cigarette smoke and his own body.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French de, from Old French de, from Latin dē, from Proto-Italic *dē, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₁, from *de + *-h₁.
Compare Portuguese quanto a, Italian (in) quanto a, Asturian and Spanish en cuanto a.

ety.text: From Latin dē. Cognate with English to. For etymology 1, preposition sense 11, compare French delà, deçà and deci delà.

es:de.gl: of; 's; used after the thing owned and before the owner

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish de, from Latin dē, from Proto-Italic *dē, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₁, from *de + *-h₁. Cognate with Ladino de.

es:en cuanto a.gl: with regard to (concerning); when it comes to

ety.text: Compare Asturian en cuanto a, Italian (in) quanto a, Portuguese quanto a and French quant à.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese de, from Latin dē, from Proto-Italic *dē, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₁, from *de + *-h₁. Cognate with Galician de.

pt:sobre.gl: on; atop; on top of (located on the top surface of)

chain.g: [of place] above; over; on the top of; upon

ety.text: From Old Galician-Portuguese sobre, from Latin super, from *eks-uper, which consists of Proto-Indo-European *eḱs (“out of”) and *uperi. Doublet of the borrowed super. Cognate to Spanish sobre, French sur, Ancient Greek ὑπέρ (hupér, “above”) and English over, super and sur-.
From Old Galician-Portuguese en, from Latin in (“in”), from Proto-Italic *en, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én (“in”). Doublet of in.
From Latin per, taking many roles from Latin pro.
From Latin versus (past participle of vertere). Cognate to French vers (“towards”).
